Project in Brief

One practical exam, five kinds of data: a table of wine measurements, a few photos, handwritten digits, a daily temperature series and plain text. This project asks which kind of network suits each one, and how much better it is than a simple baseline. It classifies wines with an ANN, uses OpenCV to select colours, clean masks, find edges and detect faces, compares a CNN with an ANN on MNIST digits, forecasts temperature with a GRU against a naive "tomorrow = today" baseline, and finishes with pre-trained Transformers for fill-mask, question answering and text generation.

94.44%test accuracy of the Wine ANN (34 of 36 wines)
97.28%test accuracy of the MNIST CNN (ANN baseline: 95.45%)
2.31 °CGRU RMSE (naive baseline: 2.49 °C)
9 / 10question-answering answers correct

All 5 Steps

Step 1Completed

ANN — Wine Classification

Classify wines into 3 classes from 13 chemical measurements.

  • No missing values. Class sizes: 59, 71 and 48 wines, so the data is fairly balanced.
  • Feature ranges differ a lot: proline runs from 278 to 1680, nonflavanoid_phenols only from 0.13 to 0.66. All features were scaled with StandardScaler, fitted on the training data only.
  • Split 142 train / 36 test (80/20, stratified, seed 42). Labels one-hot encoded (3 columns).
  • Architecture: Input 13 → Dense 16 (ReLU) → Dense 8 (ReLU) → Dense 3 (Softmax), 387 parameters. First hidden layer counted by hand: 13 × 16 + 16 = 224, matching model.summary().
  • Adam, categorical cross-entropy, 60 epochs, batch size 8, 20% validation split (29 wines). Last-epoch train and validation accuracy both reached 1.0.
  • Test accuracy 94.44%: 2 of 36 wines wrong. The three softmax outputs of a test wine add up to 1.

Step 2Completed

OpenCV — Colour, Morphology, Edges and Faces

Process five images with classic computer-vision tools, without any training.

  • Images loaded with scikit-image, converted RGB → BGR for OpenCV, resized to 256 × 256.
  • HSV conversion, then an orange mask ([10, 100, 70] to [25, 255, 255]) with cv2.inRange and cv2.bitwise_and. It keeps most of the coffee and cat images and very little of the rocket image.
  • Mask cleaned with erosion then dilation (5 × 5 kernel): tiny white dots disappear, the main shapes stay.
  • Sobel edges (x and y combined, convertScaleAbs): bright where brightness changes fast, such as object borders.
  • Haar cascade face detection (scaleFactor 1.1, minNeighbors 5): 1 face, in the astronaut image; 0 in the other four.
  • All processed images, a 5 × 5 summary grid and a face-detection row were saved in the outputs folder (32 files).
minNeighborsFaces found in the astronaut image
22 (one is a false positive)

81

A low minNeighbors accepts weak matches and gives extra boxes; a very high value can miss small or tilted faces. The fifth image is a built-in scikit-image picture (colorwheel), not a personal photo.

Step 3Completed

CNN vs ANN — MNIST Digits

Compare a small CNN with an ANN baseline on the same digit images.

  • First 20,000 training and 4,000 test images, divided by 255 and reshaped to (28, 28, 1); labels one-hot encoded (10 columns).
  • CNN: Conv 16 (3 × 3) → MaxPool → Conv 32 (3 × 3) → MaxPool → Flatten → Dense 64 → Dense 10, 56,714 parameters. ANN: Flatten → Dense 128 → Dense 64 → Dense 10, 109,386 parameters.
  • Adam, 8 epochs, batch size 64, 10% validation split. The CNN used EarlyStopping (patience 2, best weights restored): the lowest validation loss (0.0663) came at epoch 6.
  • Test accuracy: CNN 0.9728, ANN 0.9545 (+1.83 points) with about half the parameters. Precision and recall are 0.94 or higher for every digit.
  • 109 of 4,000 test digits are wrong. The most common mistake is a 7 predicted as a 2 (9 times). The first Conv2D layer gives 16 feature maps for a test digit. Model saved as cnn_mnist_model.h5.

CNN vs ANN

ModelTotal ParametersEpochsTrain AccVal AccTest Acc
CNN56,71480.99080.98100.9728
ANN109,38680.99280.96250.9545

The CNN reuses one small 3 × 3 filter over the whole image, while the ANN gives every pixel its own weight. The ANN has no callback, so its test score comes from the last epoch, where validation loss had already started to rise (lowest at epoch 5).

Step 4Completed

GRU — Temperature Forecasting

Predict the next day's minimum temperature from the previous 30 days.

  • 3,650 daily values from 1981 to 1990. The check for stray text found 0 bad values; the series repeats a yearly wave and day-to-day values are noisy.
  • First 80% for training (2,920 days), last 20% for testing (730 days), no shuffling. MinMaxScaler fitted on the training days only.
  • 30-day windows made with a loop: 2,890 train and 700 test sequences, shape (samples, 30, 1).
  • Model: GRU (32 units, tanh) → Dense 1, 3,393 parameters. Adam, MSE, 15 epochs, batch size 32, 10% validation split. About 1 s per epoch; final loss 0.0089 (train) and 0.0096 (validation), both flat after the first epochs.
  • Naive baseline: tomorrow = today. The GRU beat it by about 7% in RMSE.
  • Bonus LSTM (32 units, 4,385 parameters) scored almost the same as the GRU. GRU saved as rnn_temperature_model.h5.
ModelParametersRMSE (°C)MAE (°C)
GRU3,3932.3091.828
LSTM (bonus)4,3852.2861.802
Naive baseline—2.4861.951

RMSE and MAE are errors in degrees Celsius. The scaler was fitted on training data only so no information from the "future" test days leaked into training.

Step 5Completed

Transformers — Fill-Mask, Question Answering and Text Generation

Use pre-trained Hugging Face models without any training.

  • Fill-mask with five sentences (top 3 answers each, see table below).
  • Question answering on five short paragraphs with ten questions, one of them unanswerable. 9 of 10 answers are correct (checked against expected answers written by the author).
  • A Hinglish question ("ISRO ka headquarters kahan hai?") was answered correctly: Bengaluru, score 0.865.
  • Text generation with distilgpt2: three prompts completed twice each, then one prompt run at temperature 0.5 and 1.5. Low temperature gave safer, repeated text; high temperature gave more varied but less meaningful text. Even fluent outputs were off-topic or factually wrong.

Train and validation values are last-epoch values from the Keras log. The MNIST CNN test score uses the best-validation weights (epoch 6); the other models use their last-epoch weights. The Wine validation set has only 29 wines and the test set 36. GRU losses are on scaled (0–1) temperatures. LSTM training was run without a log, so its losses are not shown. About 2 s per epoch for the CNN and 1 s for the ANN and GRU, rounded from the Keras logs on the author's machine.

  • The CNN beat the ANN by 1.83 points with about half the parameters (56,714 vs 109,386).
  • The GRU beat the naive baseline by about 7% in RMSE; the bonus LSTM was only slightly better than the GRU.
  • The Wine ANN reached 94.44% with 387 parameters and very little code.
  • The pre-trained models answered 9 of 10 questions but got the capital of India wrong in fill-mask and answered an unanswerable question with a high score.

Which Model Should We Use?

Recommendation: pick the simplest model that beats its baseline. The CNN is the right choice for digit images (97.3% with 56,714 parameters). For temperature, the small GRU is enough: it is only a little better than "tomorrow = today", and the LSTM adds almost nothing. Pre-trained Transformers are useful without any training, but their answers must be checked.

Wine ANN

94.4% test accuracy with 387 parameters; with only 36 test wines, one mistake moves the score by 2.8 points.

MNIST CNN

97.3% accuracy and about half the ANN's parameters; best result of the exam on a harder image task.

GRU

RMSE 2.31 °C against 2.49 °C for the naive baseline; follows the yearly pattern but misses sudden jumps.

Transformers

9 of 10 correct answers, but confident wrong answers exist (capital of India, unanswerable question).

Limitations (observations only): each model was trained once, so small differences (for example GRU vs LSTM) are not conclusive; MNIST was cut to 20,000 training and 4,000 test images and trained for only 8 epochs, so scores are below a full-data run; the Wine test set has only 36 samples; the "Correct" column in Step 5 compares answers with expected answers written by the author, not with human judges; the fifth OpenCV image is a built-in picture, not a personal photo; the temperature data comes from one city.
